title: Mata Sulakhni
hookLine: Nanak's wife, whose steadiness made the travels possible
tomorrow: Mata Khivi, named in the Granth

lines: A LINE OR TWO FOR HOME.
cards: Behind a well-known journey there's often someone who didn't go. Someone who kept the lamps lit, answered the door, fed the children, and was there when the traveler came back dusty from the road.
The traveler gets the stories. The one at home gets a line or two, if that. The janamsakhis tell and retell Guru Nanak's long journeys.
The woman who stayed is mentioned far more briefly. Today, her name: Mata Sulakhni.

teach.b: Start with honesty about the sources. The janamsakhis say much more about Guru Nanak's travels than about his marriage. Mata Sulakhni appears in them, but she rarely speaks.
Tradition says she was the daughter of Mool Chand and that they married at Batala. Their sons were Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das.
Beyond that, the old stories give us her presence more than her words, and it would be wrong to fill the silence with made-up speeches. So look at what they do show.
When Guru Nanak left on his long journeys, preaching the Name far from home, someone had to keep that home standing: the children raised, the household run.
That was Mata Sulakhni, and in some tellings the family, including Bebe Nanaki, helped her.

teach.h: THE TRAVELS STAND ON HER STEADINESS.
teach.b: Without that steadiness, the travels don't happen. Nobody can carry a message across many lands if the ground behind them is falling apart. A great deal of faithful life looks like this.
Not a sermon from a mountaintop. A pot on the stove, a child's lesson checked, a door answered, day after day, while someone else's work goes out into the world.
Sikhs call her Mata, mother, as a title of honor.
Steady at home isn't the small part of the story. It's the part the rest of the story stands on.

how: Sikhs honor Mata Sulakhni as Guru Nanak's wife and the mother of Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das, and her place in his life is remembered in the tellings of his marriage and travels.

games.q: you're writing about Mata Sulakhni and the old sources give you almost none of her words. what do you do?
o: invent the speeches she probably gave.
leave her out, since there's nothing to say.
say plainly what the sources show: her steadiness at home.
games.why: it would be wrong to fill the silence with made-up speeches; what the stories show is a home kept standing.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose steadiness lets other people's lives move: a parent at home, a coworker who keeps things running, a friend who's always there.
Picture one ordinary thing they do that nobody claps for, and hold it in mind with each breath; if you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: ghar, home or household; also a word gurbani uses for the inner home.
